title: Azure and Community Guidelines on Choosing between a Skill or a Sub-Agent
gist: Azure lead engineer Kishorekumar Pattabiraman argues the first architectural decision in building AI systems is not model selection but whether a capability should be a skill (interactive, in-conversation, human-in-the-loop) or a sub-agent (single prompt, runs to completion, clean context), decided along four dimensions: iteration model, voice fidelity, human gate placement, and task frequency. Community commentary adds the context-window and orchestration-non-determinism trade-offs, and the piece closes by noting the two shapes compose — a skill built on a sub-agent is often the most mature design.

insights.claim: Azure lead engineer Kishorekumar Pattabiraman argues that teams building AI systems routinely start with the wrong question — which model to use — when the first real fork is architectural: skill or sub-agent.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: If the decisive variable in agent system quality is delivery shape rather than model, then model-benchmark differentiation matters less to buyers than vendors assume.
insights.quote: Are you building a skill or a sub-agent? Get that wrong and no model choice will save you. A skill and a sub-agent are two different delivery shapes, and each one fails at the other one's job.
insights.locator: The "first real fork" though, is not the model

insights.claim: A skill operates within an ongoing conversation — reading files, asking questions, iterating with the user and keeping a human in the loop throughout — while a sub-agent takes a single prompt, runs independently to completion, and delivers a final output.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: This is the operative definition to apply when auditing an agent architecture: check whether each component's human-interaction profile matches the shape it was built as.
insights.locator: A skill operates within an ongoing conversation

insights.claim: The skill-versus-sub-agent decision should be made along four dimensions — the iteration model, voice fidelity, human gate placement, and how frequently the task is repeated — rather than by a single rule of thumb.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A reusable four-axis checklist for reviewing any proposed agent component before it is built.
insights.locator: To decide whether to build a skill or a sub-agent

insights.claim: Of the four dimensions, task frequency produces the clearest divide: a one-off craft piece leans to a skill and a repeatable batch job to a sub-agent, while the other three require case-by-case judgement.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Frequency is the cheapest signal to measure, so use it as the first-pass classifier and reserve deeper analysis for the ambiguous cases.
insights.quote: one-off craft piece leans to a skill, a repeatable batch job to a sub-agent
insights.locator: Among the four dimensions, frequency is the one

insights.claim: The real trade-off is rarely between a fully interactive conversation and a simple handoff; it is between the cost of keeping a human engaged in an iterative skill-based flow and the risk of forcing that process into a one-shot response that must be corrected every time.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Automation ROI in agent systems should be priced as human-engagement cost versus repeated-correction cost, not as automated-versus-manual.
insights.locator: For example, the choice is rarely between a fully interactive conversation

themes.theme: Context window as the hidden constraint

insights.claim: Sub-agents always start from a clean state and do not pollute the context window, whereas a skill always carries the whole conversation with it — making context hygiene a first-order reason to choose a sub-agent.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Context-window economics, not capability, is often what actually decides agent decomposition — relevant to token cost and latency modelling.

insights.claim: The reusability case cuts the other way: a skill is reusable across multiple agents or conversation flows, while sub-agents earn their place when a step needs genuinely separate context, permissions, or a different knowledge source.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Permission boundaries and knowledge-source separation are concrete triggers for spawning a sub-agent — a useful security-review criterion, not just a design one.
insights.quote: sub-agents make sense when: the step needs genuinely separate context, permissions, or a different knowledge source
insights.locator: Another user, dan-does-ai, emphasizes different trade-offs

themes.theme: Orchestration non-determinism as an unpriced cost

insights.claim: Choosing sub-agents introduces an orchestration layer whose non-determinism is a cost distinct from and additional to the complexity it adds.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Non-determinism at the routing layer breaks reproducibility guarantees that regulated and high-stakes deployments depend on.
insights.locator: Another important consideration is the need for orchestration

insights.claim: In Copilot Studio the planner dynamically decides whether to call skills, tools, topics or sub-agents based on descriptions, context and recent conversation history, with the consequence that a skill might not be invoked on every similar prompt.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A named production platform where identical prompts can take different execution paths — treat capability invocation as probabilistic when designing tests and SLAs.
insights.quote: the planner dynamically decides when to call skills, tools, topics, or sub-agents based on descriptions, context, and recent conversation history. Because of that, a skill might not be invoked on every similar prompt.
insights.locator: For example, Reddit commenter Ashlesha-msft notes

insights.claim: Because the planner routes on component descriptions, the natural-language description attached to a skill or sub-agent becomes a load-bearing part of the system's behaviour rather than documentation.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Prompt-adjacent metadata is now production configuration — version and test descriptions the way you would code.
insights.locator: For example, Reddit commenter Ashlesha-msft notes

insights.claim: One community mental model maps the stack as an organisation: an agent is the director, a sub-agent a manager, a skill a specialized worker, a tool a dedicated machine, and MCP the governance rules or policies of the organization.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A quick communication device for explaining agent architecture to non-technical stakeholders, and a hint that MCP is being understood as a governance layer rather than merely a transport.
insights.locator: As a final perspective from the community

insights.claim: The skill-versus-sub-agent dichotomy is in many cases only apparent: the two models compose cleanly, a skill can be built on top of a sub-agent, and this layered approach often represents the most mature design.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: The mature architecture is layered rather than either/or — expect platform vendors to converge on composable primitives instead of forcing a single abstraction.

insights.claim: The decision criteria being promoted by Azure emphasise reusability, simplicity, and long-term maintainability rather than raw capability, positioning agent design as a software-engineering discipline rather than a prompt-engineering one.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Signals where enterprise AI tooling spend is heading: maintainability tooling for agent systems, not more model capability.
insights.locator: In a recent Azure Architecture blog article
